title: Add batched event delivery preserving FSEvents callback boundaries
description: FileSystemEventStream.swift:48-52 loops and calls eventHandler(event) per-event, discarding the FSEvents batch boundary. FSEvents naturally coalesces related events (e.g. atomic save = created+modified+renamed). Yield [FolderContentChangeEvent] to preserve this semantic grouping, matching Panda's approach. The existing per-event API can flatten batches for backward compatibility.
close_reason: makeBatchedStream added for url and paths; both shapes built at the source via a shared bridge helper

comments.author: Beads
comments.text:
Composes cleanly with the 2.1.0 StreamCondition work: yielding [FolderContentChangeEvent] per callback preserves the interleaving of conditions and file changes exactly as FSEvents produced it, which is required - a change reported after a MustScanSubDirs survives the rescan it demands, one before it does not. No separate channel for conditions.

Still open (Q3): does the batched form replace the per-event API or sit beside it as makeBatchedStream? Cheaper to answer once asyncfilemonitor-as7 has deleted the instance API and halved the factory matrix.

comments.author: Beads
comments.text:
Shape resolved. Batched is the primitive; per-event stays as a convenience; BOTH are built at the source, not by adapting one stream into the other.

  makeBatchedStream -> AsyncStream<[FolderContentChangeEvent]>   // yield the batch
  makeStream        -> AsyncStream<FolderContentChangeEvent>     // for event in batch { yield }

Deriving per-event by iterating the batched stream would need a task to pump between two AsyncStreams - exactly the Task hop this library exists to avoid, and the mistake the pre-2.0 static bridge made. Flattening inside the handler closure keeps both paths synchronous callback-to-continuation, so the ordering invariant holds identically on both.

Naming: keep makeStream for the per-event form so the common call site only gains 'try'.

Depends on asyncfilemonitor-p28 for the handler signature.

title: Nest FileSystemEventStreamError as FileSystemEventStream.Error
description: FileSystemEventStreamError (FileSystemEventStream.swift:16-21) is a top-level type but only thrown by FileSystemEventStream.make(). Nest it as FileSystemEventStream.Error for clearer ownership.
close_reason: Nested as FileSystemEventStream.Error; it is now internal along with its enclosing type

title: Let callers choose directory-level instead of file-level events
description: FileSystemEventStream.make always sets kFSEventStreamCreateFlagFileEvents, so every consumer pays for per-file events. A consumer that only needs to know 'something under this folder changed' would get far fewer events without the flag. Expose a granularity option (directory or file) on both makeStream forms, defaulting to file so existing behaviour is unchanged.

comments.author: Beads
comments.text: Folded into asyncfilemonitor-pn4: becomes a 'granularity' field on Configuration. Default stays .file (kFSEventStreamCreateFlagFileEvents).

comments.author: Beads
comments.text:
Implementation sketch against the 3.0 Configuration.

Field: a nested `public enum EventGranularity: Sendable { case file, directory }` plus `public var granularity: EventGranularity`, default `.file` — appended to Configuration.swift (fields at :28 and :35, memberwise init at :40-46 gains a defaulted parameter, so no call site changes).

Consumption is the flags expression, FileSystemEventStream.swift:121:

	let flags = UInt32(kFSEventStreamCreateFlagUseCFTypes | kFSEventStreamCreateFlagFileEvents)
	->
	var rawFlags = kFSEventStreamCreateFlagUseCFTypes
	if configuration.granularity == .file { rawFlags |= kFSEventStreamCreateFlagFileEvents }
	let flags = UInt32(rawFlags)

passed unchanged to `FSEventStreamCreate` at FileSystemEventStream.swift:131. `UseCFTypes` must stay unconditionally: the callback unwraps `eventPaths` as a CFArray at FileSystemEventStream.swift:57 and would crash otherwise.

The interaction that has to be settled before this ships — it is a docs/semantics problem, not a code problem:

Without `kFSEventStreamCreateFlagFileEvents` FSEvents sets no item flags at all. `Change(eventFlags:)` masks the stream bits off (Change.swift:33-34: `Int(eventFlags) & ~StreamCondition.flagsMask`), so under `.directory` an ordinary event yields an **empty** `Change`. That collides head-on with the discriminator this library documents:

- `FolderContentChangeEvent.description` treats `change.isEmpty && !condition.isEmpty` as "condition-only element" (FolderContentChangeEvent.swift:52).
- "FSEvents Flag Reference.md", section "Why a product, not a sum", states `change.isEmpty` *is* the discriminator for a condition-only element, and its consuming snippet does `guard !event.change.isEmpty else { continue }` — under `.directory` that guard drops every real event.

Per-stream this is coherent (a `.directory` consumer knows its events carry no item flags and only `eventPath` matters), but the published contract currently promises the opposite. Options to decide: document the discriminator as `.file`-only; or expose granularity on the event; or leave the discriminator alone and make it a loud caveat on the field's doc comment.

Secondary interaction: `eventPath` becomes the *directory* containing the change, not the changed item, so `FolderContentChangeEvent.url` (FolderContentChangeEvent.swift:43) points at a folder. Consumers keying on the path get a coarser key — which is the point of the option, but it is a behavioural difference worth stating.

`sinceWhen` replay and `latency` coalescing are unaffected; `mustScanSubDirectories` still arises the same way.

title: Move EventHandlerBox inside FileSystemEventStream.make()
description: EventHandlerBox (FileSystemEventStream.swift:28-34) is defined at file scope but only used inside make(). Move it to be a function-local class, matching Panda's pattern of scoping types to exactly where they're needed.
close_reason: Nested in FileSystemEventStream rather than function-local: the C callback also references EventHandlerBox, so both had to move together

title: Pass kFSEventStreamCreateFlagMarkSelf so ownEvent can fire
description:
Change.ownEvent (Change.swift) is named but unreachable: the Core Services headers set kFSEventStreamEventFlagOwnEvent only for streams created with kFSEventStreamCreateFlagMarkSelf, and FileSystemEventStream.make passes only UseCFTypes | FileEvents. Verified against the SDK header and by probe: no observed event carried 0x80000.

Enabling it gives consumers echo suppression - the ability to ignore changes their own process made, which a writer-plus-watcher (an editor saving into a folder it monitors) otherwise has to infer from paths and timing.

Sibling of asyncfilemonitor-ekx and asyncfilemonitor-nav: a Bool field on Configuration, default false to keep current behaviour, consumed in the same flags expression in FileSystemEventStream.make.

Caveat from the header: MarkSelf has no effect on historical events, i.e. those replayed before StreamCondition.historyDone. Document that alongside the field.

Until this lands, Change.ownEvent's doc comment says it is never reported.

title: Delete the multicast instance API in 3.0
description:
FolderContentMonitor's instance form (init + makeStream()) exists to let several subscribers share one FSEventStream. No consumer uses it that way: TheArchive2, the only consumer, calls makeStream() exactly once per monitor. Deleting it removes MulticastAsyncStream, StreamLifecycleEvent, the Mutex state machine and the lifecycle task, and lets every feature below be designed once instead of twice.

Decided without a deprecation cycle: 2.0.0 is a day old and the sole consumer is in-house.

Two further reasons it blocks other work. (1) On the instance path FileSystemEventStream.make runs inside the lifecycle task on first-subscriber, so there is no caller left to throw to - a throwing factory (asyncfilemonitor-xo0) cannot work there. (2) That same asynchrony means monitoring starts some time after init returns, which reopens the buffering window TheArchive2's CollectionFolderMonitor relies on being closed; the static form creates the stream synchronously in the AsyncStream build closure.

Migration for TheArchive2 is constructor + makeStream() -> FolderContentMonitor.makeStream(url:).
close_reason: Instance API, MulticastAsyncStream and StreamLifecycleEvent deleted; FolderContentMonitor is a caseless enum

comments.author: Beads
comments.text: Also in scope: FolderContentMonitor becomes a caseless enum. With the instance API gone there is nothing to instantiate, and an enum makes that a compiler-enforced fact rather than a convention. The four static factories are all that remain on it.

title: Fix silent error handling: finish continuations on FSEventStream creation failure
description: FolderContentMonitor.swift:175 just print()s when FileSystemEventStream.make() fails. Consumers get a stream that never yields and never finishes. Should call continuation.finish() (or a new finishAll() on MulticastAsyncStream) so the for-await loop ends cleanly, matching Panda's pattern.
close_reason: Both paths now finish continuations on FSEventStream creation failure

comments.author: Beads
comments.text: Half-done on main: the static makeStream path now finishes continuations on failure. The instance path still only print()s at Sources/AsyncFileMonitor/FolderContentMonitor.swift:175. Note the stashed static-makeStream slice satisfies finish() but swallows the error entirely, so consumers still cannot distinguish 'no changes' from 'failed to start' - consider an AsyncThrowingStream variant.

title: Pass kFSEventStreamCreateFlagWatchRoot so rootChanged can fire
description:
StreamCondition.rootChanged is named but unreachable: the Core Services headers state it is only ever delivered when the stream was created with kFSEventStreamCreateFlagWatchRoot, and FileSystemEventStream.make passes only UseCFTypes | FileEvents. So 'a directory along the path to the watched folder changed, and the watched path may no longer exist' is currently unobservable.

Sibling of asyncfilemonitor-nav and asyncfilemonitor-9cr: all three are creation-flag/configuration options on the same factories, so settle their shape (loose parameters vs a config struct) together. Default off to keep current behaviour.

comments.author: Beads
comments.text: Folded into asyncfilemonitor-pn4: becomes a 'watchesRoot' field on Configuration. Default stays false, i.e. current behaviour, where rootChanged never fires.

comments.author: Beads
comments.text:
Implementation sketch against the 3.0 Configuration.

Field: `public var watchesRoot: Bool`, default `false` — i.e. today's behaviour, where `rootChanged` never fires. Appended to Configuration.swift alongside `sinceWhen` (:28) and `latency` (:35); the memberwise init at :40-46 gains a defaulted parameter.

Consumption is the same flags expression as asyncfilemonitor-9cr, FileSystemEventStream.swift:121:

	let flags = UInt32(kFSEventStreamCreateFlagUseCFTypes | kFSEventStreamCreateFlagFileEvents)
	->
	var rawFlags = kFSEventStreamCreateFlagUseCFTypes | kFSEventStreamCreateFlagFileEvents
	if configuration.watchesRoot { rawFlags |= kFSEventStreamCreateFlagWatchRoot }
	let flags = UInt32(rawFlags)

Since both this and 9cr edit line 121, land them together or accept a trivial conflict.

Why the flag is the whole feature: `StreamCondition.rootChanged` (StreamCondition.swift:75) is already defined and already decoded by `StreamCondition(eventFlags:)` (StreamCondition.swift:33) and named by `description` (StreamCondition.swift:115). No parsing work is needed. The bit is simply never set, because the headers only ever send it for a stream created with `kFSEventStreamCreateFlagWatchRoot` — noted at StreamCondition.swift:73-75 and in "FSEvents Flag Reference.md" ("RootChanged is **unreachable as configured**"). Passing the creation flag is the single change that makes the case reachable at all.

Event ID zero: rootChanged events carry event ID 0 (StreamCondition.swift:69, flag reference Group B). This matters for anyone persisting `FolderContentChangeEvent.eventID` as a `sinceWhen` resume point (Configuration.swift:20-27): a naive `lastSeen = event.eventID` would rewind the resume point to 0 and replay the entire history on the next start. So the docs must say: skip id-0 events when recording a resume point. Worth a test that a rootChanged element does not poison a max-eventID accumulator.

Path semantics do need documenting, yes:
- `eventPath` on a rootChanged event is the *monitored* path as it was passed in, not the new location. There is no rename target in the event.
- The watched path may no longer exist, or may now be a different directory. FSEvents keeps following the original inode; this library cannot re-point the stream, because `paths` is baked into `FSEventStreamCreate` (FileSystemEventStream.swift:124-132) and `FileSystemEventStream` is `~Copyable` with no mutation path.
- Therefore recovery is the caller's job: on `rootChanged`, stat the path, and if it is gone or replaced, break iteration and call `makeStream` again for the new location. That recipe belongs in the docs (UnderstandingEvents / the flag reference) next to the field.
- With multiple `paths`, rootChanged identifies which one via `eventPath`.

Two doc sites go stale the moment this lands and must be updated in the same change:
- StreamCondition.swift:73-75, "which this library does not currently pass".
- "FSEvents Flag Reference.md" Group B, the "unreachable as configured" paragraph and its "tracked separately" pointer (this issue).

title: Let callers choose the AsyncStream buffering policy
description:
FolderContentMonitor's private bridge helper uses AsyncStream.makeStream() with the default .unbounded buffering policy, so a consumer slower than the event rate grows the buffer without limit. Watching a busy tree (a build directory, a sync target) while doing per-event async work is the realistic case.

Configuration is the natural home: a bufferingPolicy field defaulting to .unbounded keeps current behaviour and is source-compatible, so this can land in a 3.x minor.

Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default: dropping events silently is its own hazard for a consumer reconciling against a baseline, and .bufferingNewest(n) would discard exactly the StreamCondition.mustScanSubDirectories element that tells them to re-list. Whatever the default, the interaction with stream conditions needs documenting.

title: Let callers choose the event delivery queue's QoS
description: FileSystemEventStream.make hardcodes DispatchQueue(label: "FileSystemEventStream", qos: .userInteractive). That suits a UI observing a folder the user is looking at, but a background indexer or sync process would reasonably want a lower QoS so event delivery does not compete with foreground work. Expose qos as a parameter on both makeStream forms, defaulting to .userInteractive so existing behaviour is unchanged.

comments.author: Beads
comments.text: Folded into asyncfilemonitor-pn4: becomes a 'qos' field on Configuration rather than a parameter on four signatures. Default stays .userInteractive.

comments.author: Beads
comments.text:
Implementation sketch against the 3.0 Configuration.

Field: `public var qos: DispatchQoS`, default `.userInteractive` — a new stored property on FolderContentMonitor.Configuration (Configuration.swift:35 is the last field today; the memberwise init at Configuration.swift:40-46 grows a third defaulted parameter, so every existing call site keeps compiling).

Sendability checked, not assumed: `DispatchQoS` itself conforms to Sendable (compiles clean under `swift -swift-version 6`), so the field can be the full `DispatchQoS` rather than the narrower `DispatchQoS.QoSClass`. Full `DispatchQoS` also carries `relativePriority`, which `DispatchQueue(label:qos:)` accepts directly.

Consumption is a single expression, FileSystemEventStream.swift:103:

	let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "FileSystemEventStream", qos: .userInteractive)
	->
	let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "FileSystemEventStream", qos: configuration.qos)

Nothing else in `make` reads the queue except `FSEventStreamSetDispatchQueue(stream, queue)` at FileSystemEventStream.swift:137, and the queue is stored on the struct (FileSystemEventStream.swift:82) only to keep it alive.

Interactions worth flagging:

- Ordering is unaffected. QoS changes *when* the callback runs, not the order: the callback still delivers a whole batch synchronously on one serial queue (FileSystemEventStream.swift:54-79), and the no-Task-hop invariant lives in `deliver` (FolderContentMonitor.swift:130-136), not in the queue's priority.
- Consumer-side priority is not covered by this. The consumer awaiting the AsyncStream runs on its own executor; lowering `qos` throttles the FSEvents callback and the `continuation.yield`, not the `for await` body.
- Teardown inherits the queue too: `deinit` calls `FSEventStreamStop`, which blocks until in-flight callbacks return (FileSystemEventStream.swift:148-153, warning at :162-164). A `.background` queue makes that block potentially longer, so the documented "do not release the box from inside an event handler" hazard gets more expensive, not different in kind.
- The label stays constant, so two streams with different QoS are indistinguishable in Instruments. Consider interpolating the QoS class into the label, or leave as-is and note it.

title: Batch the internal event handler signature
description:
FileSystemEventStream's C callback loops over numEvents and calls eventHandler once per event, discarding the FSEvents batch boundary before anything can use it. Change the handler to @Sendable ([FolderContentChangeEvent]) -> Void and build the array once per callback invocation.

Internal only - no public signature changes - so it can land ahead of the 3.0 work and unblocks asyncfilemonitor-2vi. The two current call sites each become a one-line closure: yield the batch, or loop and yield each element.
close_reason: Handler now takes [FolderContentChangeEvent] per callback; both call sites flatten locally

title: Replace loose factory parameters with a Configuration struct
close_reason: Configuration struct introduced; nav/9cr/ekx are now field additions

title: Throw instead of trapping when a URL is not a file URL
description:
FolderContentMonitor.makeStream(url:configuration:) and makeBatchedStream(url:configuration:) call precondition(url.isFileURL), which traps the process. That predates 3.0, when nothing in the API could report a problem; now that the factories throw a typed FolderContentMonitor.Error, trapping is inconsistent with the rest of the surface.

A URL can come from user input, a document picker, a pasted string or a restored bookmark, so a non-file URL is a recoverable input error rather than a programmer error, and a library should not take the process down for it.

Add case notAFileURL to FolderContentMonitor.Error and replace both preconditions with a throw. Source-compatible for callers that already handle the thrown error, since the factories are already throwing -- so this can ship in 3.1 rather than waiting for 4.0.

Note the paths: [String] factories have no equivalent check; decide whether they should validate too, or whether the URL overloads are the only place it belongs.

title: Surface FSEventStream creation failure to consumers instead of print()
description: Both makeStream paths now finish() the stream when FileSystemEventStream.make() fails (asyncfilemonitor-dee), but the error itself only reaches a print(). Consumers still cannot distinguish 'watched folder had no changes' from 'monitoring never started'. Consider an AsyncThrowingStream variant, or a throwing factory, so the failure is part of the API rather than a log line.
close_reason: Factories throw a typed FolderContentMonitor.Error; failure is reported at construction rather than as a log line

comments.author: Beads
comments.text: Consumer demand registered from TheArchive2 (ta2-coder), which adopted 2.0.0 with no call-site changes. They journal when the event stream finishes without their own teardown having cancelled it, so a collection whose FSEventStream never started now leaves a trace instead of silently losing external-change monitoring. That distinguishes 'died' from 'torn down' but not why it died. What they want: a typed reason on stream finish, or an error event, so the journal line can name the failure. No urgency stated. Panda's FolderMonitor.makeEventStream is a reference point for the minimum bar - it calls log.error on setup failure where we print().

comments.author: Beads
comments.text:
Design resolved in planning; blocked on asyncfilemonitor-as7.

Two distinct failure modes were conflated here. Mid-stream degradation (FSEvents dropping events) shipped in 2.1.0 as StreamCondition - see docs/FSEvents Flag Reference.md. This issue is now only about STARTUP failure: create/start fails and monitoring never begins.

Recommended shape: a throwing factory returning a plain AsyncStream. Not AsyncThrowingStream, not an error-as-element case.

Why it works: FSEvents can only fail at create/start, never mid-stream via the callback, and AsyncStream's build closure runs synchronously at construction (verified). So the failure is available on the caller's thread at the call site. Build it with AsyncStream.makeStream() rather than the trailing-closure init, which cannot rethrow.

This satisfies TheArchive2's recorded demand better than a typed finish reason: if construction succeeded, the stream can only finish through consumer teardown, so 'died' vs 'torn down' stops being ambiguous by construction. Cost to them: CollectionFolderMonitor.init is non-throwing today and would need to throw or catch.

title: Share one FSEventStream per path across the process
description:
Parked idea raised while deciding the fate of the instance API. Today two observers of the same folder create two kernel streams, coalesced independently, so their event IDs and batch boundaries differ. A path-keyed registry would give one stream per path per process: fewer kernel resources, and identical events for all observers of a path.

This is what the multicast machinery would actually be good for - note the instance API does NOT do it today (each instance owns its own stream). Deliberately not a reason to keep the instance API; revisit after 3.0. Changes observable semantics, so it needs its own design pass.

comments.author: Beads
comments.text:
Design problem, not a proposal. Writing down what a path-keyed registry would actually have to solve, because the answer may be that it should not exist.

1. What is the key?

`makeStream(paths:)` takes `[String]` (FolderContentMonitor.swift:75-78, :116-119), so the unit is a path *set*, not a path. Before any sharing can happen:
- Canonicalization: symlinks, trailing slashes, `.`/`..`, APFS case-insensitivity, `/private/var` vs `/var`. Two callers naming the same directory differently must hit the same key or the registry silently does nothing.
- Nesting: `/a` and `/a/b` are not the same key, but a stream on `/a` already reports everything a stream on `/a/b` would. Merging them means the `/a/b` caller now receives (and must filter) events for the whole of `/a`, and hierarchical coalescing means a `mustScanSubDirectories` for `/a` is *not* equivalent to one for `/a/b` (see "FSEvents Flag Reference.md", Group A: a change in one subtree can surface as a single event for the parent). So merging changes what the narrower caller sees.
- Set overlap: `[A, B]` and `[B, C]` share nothing keyable without splitting into per-path streams and re-fanning — which is a different, bigger design.

2. Configuration cannot be reconciled between sharers — this is the load-bearing objection.

Every Configuration field is an argument to `FSEventStreamCreate` (FileSystemEventStream.swift:124-132) and is fixed for the life of the kernel stream:
- `latency` (Configuration.swift:35) defines the coalescing window. Two callers wanting 0 and 2.0 cannot share; picking the min gives the 2.0 caller more callbacks than requested, the max makes the 0 caller late. There is no post-hoc split: coalescing destroys information, and re-coalescing on the consumer side is not the same thing.
- `sinceWhen` (Configuration.swift:28) is worse. A sharer that asked for `kFSEventStreamEventIdSinceNow` joining a stream created with a historical resume point would receive replayed history plus a `historyDone` sentinel it never asked for; joining *after* the replay means the resuming caller's own guarantee ("everything since ID N") cannot be offered to a late joiner at all. Sharing has no correct answer here, only a choice of which caller to break.
- Once asyncfilemonitor-nav, -9cr and -ekx land, `qos`, `granularity` and `watchesRoot` join the list — all creation-time, all unshareable across callers who disagree.

So the key degenerates to (canonical path set, entire Configuration), and sharing only ever happens between requests that are identical in every respect. That is a much smaller win than "one stream per path", and it is the only version that is semantically coherent. State plainly: a process-wide *per-path* registry is incoherent given per-caller Configuration.

3. Lifecycle and teardown races.

Today teardown is pure RAII with no shared state: `EventStreamBox` is captured by `continuation.onTermination` (FolderContentMonitor.swift:143-151) and the kernel stream dies in `deinit` (FileSystemEventStream.swift:148-153). A registry replaces this with refcounting and inherits a documented hazard: `FSEventStreamStop` blocks until in-flight callbacks on the stream's queue have returned, and releasing the last reference *from that queue* deadlocks (FileSystemEventStream.swift:161-164). With sharing, the last release is no longer under the control of the caller who created the stream — any subscriber's teardown can become the one that blocks, from any thread.
Races to specify: last-unsubscriber-decrements-to-zero concurrent with a new subscriber arriving for the same key (resurrect the entry or create a second stream?), and eviction ordering versus a callback already in flight. This wants a lock held across both the refcount change and the map mutation, without holding it across `FSEventStreamStop`.
It also breaks the one existing observable teardown proof: `FileSystemEventStream.liveCount` (FileSystemEventStream.swift:22-26) currently equals the number of live consumer streams, and the lifecycle leak tests assert on that. Under sharing it equals the number of live *keys*, so those tests need a new invariant.

4. Observable semantics that change.

- Identical event IDs and batch boundaries across sharers is the stated goal, but it is a behaviour change: today two observers of one folder coalesce independently and legitimately see different batching (FolderContentMonitor.makeBatchedStream, FolderContentMonitor.swift:99-121).
- Backpressure/fan-out: one slow consumer's `continuation.yield` now sits on the queue shared with everyone else's delivery. Today a slow consumer only slows its own stream.
- `OwnEvent`, dropped-event conditions and `mustScanSubDirectories` become shared facts: one sharer's dropped events are reported to all.
- Per-subscriber start time: a late joiner attaches mid-stream and can never be told "you have seen everything since you subscribed" the way a fresh `FSEventStreamCreate` with `sinceWhen` can.

5. Verdict to carry into any future design pass.

The coherent form is share-per-(canonical path set, full Configuration), which mostly evaporates the benefit — the common case is a handful of observers with the default Configuration on the same folder, which is real but narrow. Weigh that narrow win against: a global mutable registry in a library that currently has none, a new class of teardown race on top of an already documented deadlock hazard, and the loss of per-consumer isolation. Kernel-stream cost is the only hard argument for it, and it should be measured before any of the above is built.

title: Make MulticastAsyncStream, StreamLifecycleEvent, and FileSystemEventStreamError internal
description: These types are implementation details never used by consumers. Making them internal cleans up the public API surface. Currently public at: MulticastAsyncStream.swift:43, MulticastAsyncStream.swift:22, FileSystemEventStream.swift:16.
close_reason: MulticastAsyncStream, StreamLifecycleEvent and the stream error are internal; docc topics updated
